lessons.title: Brokerage, STT, Stamp Duty, and SEBI Charges Explained Line by Line

children.text: Chapter 1 walked through the anatomy of a single equity delivery trade. Most quant analyst aspirants and prop trading applicants do not trade cash equity delivery alone, they build strategies across intraday equity, futures, and options too, and each segment prices these six charges differently. This lesson is the reference: precise definitions, and the exact rates for each segment, in one place.

body.title: Explicit Transaction Costs, One at a Time

cards.definition: The fee your broker charges for executing an order. Not statutory, set entirely by the broker. Discount brokers like Zerodha and Groww typically charge ₹0 on equity delivery and a flat fee (commonly around ₹20) or a small percentage, whichever is lower, on intraday and F&O.

A central government tax on securities transactions, computed on trade value for equity and futures, and on premium value for options. Rate and which side (buy, sell, or both) it applies to differs by segment.

A fee levied by NSE or BSE for every executed order, to cover the cost of running the exchange and matching engine. Differs by segment and, in options, is computed on premium value rather than notional.
A very small regulatory fee, commonly cited as ₹10 per crore of turnover, charged by SEBI across segments to fund market regulation.
A state-levied duty, unified into a single nationwide rate schedule since July 2020, charged only on the buy side, with a different rate for each segment.
Central Goods and Services Tax, charged at 18% on brokerage, exchange transaction charges, and SEBI fees combined. Not charged on STT or stamp duty, since those are themselves taxes.

body.text: These rates reflect recent, commonly cited levels, including the STT increase on futures and options that took effect from October 2024. Every one of these figures, STT, exchange transaction charges, SEBI fees, stamp duty, and GST, is set by a government, exchange, or regulatory body and can change in a future Union Budget or circular. Verify current rates on your broker's charges page or the exchange's circulars before wiring this into a live cost model.

children.text: Worked Comparison: Cost as a Share of Notional vs Cost as a Share of Premium

Take a futures position with ₹18,00,000 of notional value, and an options position with ₹11,250 of premium at risk but similar underlying exposure. Exact lot sizes and premium levels shift as NSE periodically revises contract specifications, so treat the rupee figures below as illustrative, and the structural point they make as the part worth remembering. Assume, as before, that the price is unchanged from entry to exit, to isolate the pure cost of the round trip.

body.text: Options STT, exchange charges, and stamp duty are all computed on premium, not on the notional exposure the option controls. That makes options look almost costless against notional, roughly 15 times cheaper than futures in the example above, but expensive against the capital actually at risk, since premium is a small fraction of notional. A strategy that trades options frequently and evaluates cost against notional exposure will badly understate what it is really paying. Always measure options trading cost against premium, not notional.

body.title: Quick Check
body.prompt: You sell a Nifty options position for ₹50,000 in premium. STT on an options sell is charged at 0.1% of premium value. How much STT, in rupees, do you pay on this sell order?
body.explanation: 0.1% of ₹50,000 is ₹50. Because options STT applies only to the sell side, no STT is charged again when you originally bought to open this position, only the other charges that apply to the buy side, such as stamp duty.

body.text: The same six charges apply across cash equity, futures, and options, but the rate, the side they apply to, and what they are computed on all change by segment. Get the base wrong, premium instead of notional for options being the classic mistake, and your cost model will be wrong by an order of magnitude even if every rate you used was correct.

points: The six charges, brokerage, STT, exchange transaction charges, SEBI fees, stamp duty, and GST, apply across every segment, but their rate and which side they hit changes segment by segment.
STT on futures and options is charged only on the sell side, at 0.02% of notional for futures and 0.1% of premium for options, following the rate increase effective October 2024.

Options charges are computed on premium value, not on the notional exposure the option controls, which makes options look far cheaper than futures against notional but considerably more expensive against the capital actually at risk.

All of these rates are set by government, exchange, or regulatory bodies, and change periodically, so a cost model should reference current rates rather than the specific figures quoted in this lesson.
